tagline: Back roads link coal towns, pine forests and handmade milling machinery
intro: The Swiftwater Corridor takes back roads through pine forestland, historic towns and valley cattle ranches. Designated a Washington State Scenic and Recreational Highway, it links Salmon La Sac with Ellensburg. Scenic Washington presents a longer journey continuing to Vantage on the Columbia River, highlighting communities bypassed by faster traffic. Near Thorp, the high forests of the Cascade Range give way to fields growing timothy hay and alfalfa, a change from the coal towns farther up the corridor.

Highway travel changed these towns alongside the railroads and mines. In 1913, state highway funding supported construction of the Sunset Highway between Seattle and Spokane, with its route passing directly through Cle Elum’s business district. Farther east, US 10 ran north of Thorp in 1926; Interstate 90 opened in 1968. The scenic corridor now includes SR 10, the former US 10.

Begin at Salmon La Sac, between the Cle Elum and Cooper rivers, then continue through Roslyn to Cle Elum. The route follows SR 970 and SR 10 toward Thorp, passing their junction at Teanaway. At Thorp, high forests give way to ranches and farmland. The mill’s handmade wooden machinery anchors a stop before the corridor continues toward Ellensburg.

moments.title: Roslyn
moments.text: Roslyn’s 26 adjoining cemetery plots reflect the varied immigrant communities of a coal town founded in 1886. Its mines supplied coal for Northern Pacific railway construction and continued railroad operations. Workers came from Italy, Poland, Slovakia and other European countries. As diesel replaced coal-fired steam trains, mining became unprofitable; the last local mine closed in 1963. Buildings from the coal years remain, including the Northwestern Improvement Company Store at First Street and Pennsylvania Avenue. Later, Roslyn and its surroundings supplied the exterior scenes of fictional Cicely, Alaska, for Northern Exposure.

moments.title: Cle Elum
moments.text: The name Cle Elum began on a railroad depot as Clealum in 1886, drawn from the Kittitas name Tle-el-Lum, meaning “swift water.” The spelling became two words in 1908. The river behind the town’s name meets the Yakima River near the town. A decade later, fire destroyed 29 city blocks, including 30 businesses and 205 houses. The 1906 Cle Elum State Bank Building survived. Downtown was quickly rebuilt in brick, and many of those buildings remain. The bank and the rebuilt streetscape mark two different chapters in the town’s surviving architecture.

moments.title: Thorp Mill
moments.text: Thorp Mill retains handmade wooden machinery from a business that milled flour for Kittitas Valley residents from 1883 until 1946. Water diverted from the Yakima through canals powered a horizontal wheel shared by the gristmill and a neighboring sawmill. Farmers brought wheat by wagon to be ground into flour, bran or livestock feed. The first grinding stones came by wagon from The Dalles, Oregon. When the Northern Pacific depot arrived in 1895, the railway enabled the installation of more efficient steel rollers and gave farmers a route to Puget Sound markets.
moments.notice: Look for the collection of handmade wooden mill machinery.
